title: Biophilia: Does Visual Contact with Nature Impact on Health and Well-Being?
review_question: Does visual contact with nature impact human health and well-being?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Evaluation of approximately fifty relevant empirical studies, focusing primarily on recent work published in established scientific journals. The review focuses on visual impact of plants, acknowledging but not prioritizing non-visual aspects like fragrance or air quality.

evidence_base_summary.date_range: Focus on recent work, but includes historical examples (e.g., ancient Egypt, Pompeii) and studies up to 2009.

findings.consequent: Negative effect on health and quality of life
findings.quote: It is concluded that an environment devoid of Nature may act as a “discord", i.e., have a negative effect.

findings.antecedent: Visual presence of plants (e.g., parks, window views, potted plants)
findings.consequent: Amelioration of negative effects of nature-deprived environments
findings.quote: The problem is partly due to the visual absence of plants, and may be ameliorated by adding elements of Nature, e.g., by creating parks, by offering a view through windows, and by potted plants.

findings.consequent: Psychological benefits (stress reduction, attention improvement, mental restoration, coping with attention deficits)
findings.quote: More specifically, contact with Nature has been reported to have psychological benefits by reducing stress [12,22], improving attention [16], by having a positive effect on mental restoration [23-25], and by coping with attention deficits [26,27].

findings.consequent: Physical health benefits (increased longevity, self-reported health)
findings.quote: In addition to mental advantages, there appear to be direct physical health benefits [28], such as increased longevity [29], and self-reported health [30,31].

findings.antecedent: View of natural landscapes (actual or in pictures)
findings.consequent: Psychological and health benefits (stress reduction, improved healing, reduced pain medication, faster recovery from surgery)
findings.quote: It has been reported that viewing natural landscapes provides psychological and health benefits, including a reduction in stress [12,13,45]. Having a hospital window with a view has been shown to improve healing, reflected in both the level of pain medication and the speed of recovery after surgery [48,49].

findings.antecedent: Indoor plants or pictures of Nature (in workplaces)
findings.quote: In the same study population it was found that having a view to plants from the work station decreased the amount of self-reported sick leave [53].
Several studies indicated that indoor plants improve the attractiveness of a room [55-58].
Other studies also indicate lower stress level when adding plants to a windowless work environment [22,59].

The biophilia hypothesis might suggest an impact of plants on emotional states; however, several studies have failed to find any consistent impact [56,60-62]. Some studies, using mood scales including several items, found significant differences, but only on particular items [57,59,63].
All the studies concluded that the subjects had better tolerance for pain with than without plants present.
One report [64] suggested that flowering plants have more positive effects on pain tolerance and distress than non-flowering plants.

Positive effects of plants were reported, although the results are somewhat ambiguous. One report found that performance on a letter identification task decreased with the presence of a larger number of plants, which was taken to suggest that fascination with plants may interfere with the focus on the task at hand [56].

A decrease in health complaints, such as tiredness and coughing, has been reported in office and hospital workers when plants were added to the work environment [67,68]. Similar findings on conceived health and level of discomfort were observed in school children [68].

findings.antecedent: Indoor plants (compared to other aesthetic objects like designer lamps or abstract pictures)
findings.consequent: Attention holding power and relief from pain
findings.quote: A study by Lohr and Pearson-Mims [63], however, suggests that plants may have advantages. They found that plants had greater attention holding power and gave greater relief from pain compared to other aesthetic objects such as a designer lamp or an abstract picture.
green spaces perceived to be unmanaged may have an adverse effect in the cities by causing an increased anxiety for crime [70].

findings.consequent: Response to plants (stronger response in women)
findings.quote: Although the results were somewhat mixed, there seemed to be a tendency for women to respond stronger to plants than men.

synthesis_conclusions: The biophilia hypothesis, suggesting an inherent human inclination to affiliate with Nature, is reasonably well substantiated by empirical evidence.
An environment devoid of Nature can act as a 'discord,' negatively impacting health and well-being, partly due to the visual absence of plants.
Adding elements of Nature, whether through outdoor experiences, therapeutic horticulture, window views, or indoor plants, can ameliorate these negative effects.
Visual contact with Nature is a sufficient, though not exclusive, mechanism for these benefits, contributing to stress relief, mental restoration, and improved mood.

While indoor plants offer benefits like improved room attractiveness, reduced stress, and enhanced pain tolerance, their effects on mood and task performance are mixed, and they are generally less potent than outdoor Nature.

The benefits of Nature, even if minor, can accumulate over a lifetime and contribute to a substantial decrease in the global health burden, making interaction with plants a worthwhile environmental initiative.
evidence_gaps: More research is needed to define the specific effects of indoor plants due to mixed results.
Most studies span short time-periods, while the full consequences of nature-deprivation may be apparent over a lifetime.
Understanding the specific mechanisms by which visual contact with plants elicits effects is limited.
publication_bias: The authors acknowledge that publications are liable to the bias of preferential reporting of positive results, which could influence the perceived consistency of findings.

moderators.effect: Women, particularly those with preinduced stress, tend to show stronger positive responses to plants than men, possibly due to evolutionary roles (gathering vs. hunting) or cultural biases (caring for home/garden).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Women showed more benefit from plants, especially with preinduced stress.

limitations: The review focuses primarily on the visual impact of plants, acknowledging but not deeply exploring other factors like fragrance or air quality.
Most studies reviewed span short time-periods, which may not capture long-term effects of nature exposure or deprivation.
The authors acknowledge the potential for publication bias, where positive results are more likely to be reported.

While the term mismatch is used for any difference between present living conditions and the environment of evolutionary adaptation, discords are mismatches with a potentially undesirable impact on health or quality of life. The problem is partly due to the visual absence of plants, and may be ameliorated by adding elements of Nature, e.g., by creating parks, by offering a view through windows, and by potted plants. The conclusion is based on an evaluation of some fifty relevant empirical studies.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Humans possess an innate tendency to connect with nature and other living systems, which is beneficial for their health and well-being.
Natural environments facilitate the restoration of directed attention, leading to improved cognitive function and reduced mental fatigue.
Exposure to natural environments reduces physiological and psychological stress more effectively than exposure to urban environments.

mechanism_chain.description: Visual contact with natural elements triggers innate biophilic responses, leading to reduced stress, restored attention, and positive emotional states, which collectively contribute to improved health and well-being.
